newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Faith spurs Singapore political maverick.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Faith spurs Singapore political maverick.

text.p: Chee Soon Juan doesn't look like a rebel.
Sitting in his comfortable office, the impeccably dressed Chee appears to be the very image of a successful young Asian businessman.

But Chee's future seems less than rosy. He faces formidable hurdles such as scathing criticism from government ministers, attacks from Singapore's media, financial ruin, and a legal case that could result in a prison term.
Chee is secretary-general of the opposition Singapore Democratic Party (SDP) and the highest-profile opponent of the island's long-running People's Action Party (PAP) government.
But the price of his political activities has been heavy.
"People say, 'Oh, he's stupid. He had a good job at the university. Why did he join the opposition?'" Chee told Reuters in an interview. "I was, I think the word is, a maverick."
Chee joined the SDP in 1992 and was one of four SDP candidates on a slate standing against a team headed by Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong in a by-election held the same year.
Three months later he was sacked from his position as a lecturer at the National University of Singapore (NUS) for the alleged misuse of research funds for postage.
"I was subsequently sued by three NUS officials for defamation concerning remarks I made (over) my dismissal."
He lost the case and had to sell his house to pay the Singapore $450,000 (US$319,000) in costs and damages.
Since then his name has rarely been out of the local papers, often as the target for attacks by the PAP or its supporters.
In recent weeks, Chee has been charged with contempt of parliament for giving false evidence to a parliamentary inquiry on the cost of living.
If found guilty by parliament, Chee and three fellow SDP members could be fined up to S$50,000 each or jailed.
A third-generation Singaporean Chinese, Chee was brought up in a Singapore undergoing immense political and economic changes.
Under its first prime minister and PAP patriarch Lee Kuan Yew, Singapore was transformed from a colonial outpost into an Asian "Tiger" with one of the world's biggest financial centres.

Since Chee was born in 1962, the economy has grown eight percent to nine percent a year, making Singaporeans on average seven times richer and bringing per capita income to US$24,000, the ninth highest in the world.
Like most of his generation, Chee benefited from Lee's social policies and went on to university in the United States where he gained a doctorate in psychology.
But he became disillusioned with what he saw as the PAP's authoritarianism, and its heavyhanded approach to political opponents and criticism.
"Arguably, what happened in the past 20 to 30 years with an authoritarian government was necessary to develop to the state we now have," said Chee.
"But the style of authoritarian government in Singapore cannot continue if we are going to compete with developed countries in future."
Chee maintains that, whatever his fate, Singapore needs to become more open and develop a free press if it is to prosper.
"As we go into the 21st century we are beginning to have to compete on ideas and creativity and enterprise. I think an authoritarian government works against this culture.
"This country needs people who dare to speak up for the things they believe are right," he said.
Chee says his Christian faith helped convert his passive criticism into political opposition.
"The New Testament always tells us that justice is important, as is fairness. These are certain values that run in the core of what I believe in," he said.
He says many Singaporeans support what he, and the social-democratic SDP, have to say.
The SDP got between 48 and 49 percent of the vote in the handful of seats it fought in the last general election in 1991.
The party now has three of the four opposition seats in Singapore's 81-seat parliament with the PAP holding the rest.
